To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the choroid plexi in the developing brain are able to secrete cerebro-spinal fluid and to transfer molecules from blood across the epithelial cells; (2) the route of transfer appears to be transcelluar; (3) the transfer of proteins is more complex than that of dextrans, and is not complete until the animal has reached adulthood.

protein and lipid insoluble molecules are transferred by separate transcellular mechanisms across the developing choroidal epithelium.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of the choroid plexues, which are responsible for the secretion of cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF).
the development of the choroid plexues in the brain, and the mechanisms by which proteins are transferred from the blood to the cerebrospinal fluids (CSF).

the development and function of the choroid plexi, the epithelial cells of which produce cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF), and which are the major sites for transport of molecules between blood and the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

in the choroid plexi of the developing brain, the epithelial cells are able to transfer both exogenous and endogenous plasma proteins across the epithelium, but that this is a relatively inefficient process.

in the developing brain, the choroid plexi are a site for the transcellular transfer of plasma proteins from blood into the CSF, and for the bidirectional transcellular transfer and the paracellular efflux of plasma proteins from the CSF into the blood.
the transfer of proteins across the epithelial cell is a dynamic process, which is not only age‐dependent but also dependent upon the molecular weight of the molecule being transferred.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the choroid plexes of developing Monodelphis domestics (opossums) are able to transfer plasma proteins and dextran markers into the cerebrospinal fluids.
the choroidal epithelium is an effective barrier to the passage of plasma proteins from the blood into the CSF, but that it is also a site for selective transport of plasma proteins into the CSF.

in the developing choroid, protein transfer occurs across the epithelial cells, whereas dextran transfer occurs through a paracellular route, which becomes increasingly effective as the choroid matures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the choroid plexi are a dynamic organ, and the mechanisms by which they secrete CSF and transport substances across the blood-CSF barrier change during development.
choroid plexi are functional early in development and that the transfer of macromolecular markers across the epithelium is by two different mechanisms.
the developing choroid epithelium is capable of transferring macromolecules across its cells from blood to CSF.
